strengths: Amortizing optimal transport across distribution pairs and resolutions is a useful objective. Combining an FNO predictor, adversarially generated training measures, and short Sinkhorn targets is a meaningful contribution beyond dataset-specific learned initializations, even though the individual ingredients are established.

The initialization experiments show substantial reductions in Sinkhorn iterations across unseen image datasets and cross-dataset pairs. Table 2 reports 2.75–3.4× speedups on the 64×64 benchmarks. The appendix adds resolution and regularization sweeps, as well as marginal-feasibility curves, providing evidence of practical value in the tested setting.

Predicting one dual potential exploits Sinkhorn's structure and permits subsequent iterative refinement. Proposition 5 provides a useful residual-to-potential-error bound under positive-kernel and centering assumptions, motivating the bootstrap targets. This is a consistency argument, however, rather than a convergence guarantee for the adversarial training procedure.

The manuscript provides architecture details, hyperparameters, pseudocode, training costs, and a code/model-weights link. It also acknowledges the fixed-cost restriction and deterioration when extrapolating to substantially higher resolutions.
weaknesses: The generator theory contains substantive errors. Theorem 3 uses a global inverse and density despite ReLU being noninvertible and introducing singular mass on the boundary; an interior, almost-everywhere formulation is needed. More decisively, Corollary 4 is false: in one dimension, G1(z)=ReLU(z/2+1) and G2(z)=ReLU(z/2) satisfy the stated residual-network assumptions, but G1(G2(z)) is always at least 1, so its distribution cannot have positive density throughout the positive orthant. This invalidates the advertised extension to compositions.

The universality theorem also does not establish coverage for the implemented generator. Appendix C uses 200 latent coordinates to generate 8,192 output coordinates and explicitly does not enforce the required Lipschitz constraint. A Lipschitz map of this lower-dimensional latent space cannot produce the claimed full-dimensional density over pairs of probability vectors. The manuscript acknowledges these differences but nevertheless concludes that generator coverage cannot bottleneck performance. That conclusion does not follow from the theorem.

The OT objectives and dual-potential conventions are inconsistent. Equation (1) requires a positive KL penalty to match the entropic dual and Sinkhorn algorithm. Beyond this likely sign typo, Algorithm 1 returns only the transport cost <C,Π>, whereas the Sinkhorn-divergence identities require the regularized optimal value. Proposition 1 also identifies scaling potentials with the potentials of the product-measure-reference dual (3) without the necessary marginal-mass factors. These distinctions affect both the interpretation of reported errors and the application of Proposition 2 to the actual prediction targets.

The geometry algorithms have correctness problems. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to an updated probability vector; this is not the stated projected-gradient method. At a nonuniform optimum with zero gradient, it still changes the solution: softmax((0.9,0.1)) is approximately (0.69,0.31). A valid simplex projection, mirror-descent update, or explicitly defined logit parameterization is needed. In addition, Appendix A.4 differentiates only the outer cross-transport term and omits the outer Sinkhorn-divergence self-interaction term. These issues undermine the mathematical basis and reproducibility of the barycenter and particle-flow demonstrations.

The contribution of the proposed training components is insufficiently isolated. There are no controlled comparisons of adversarial versus fixed random generators, bootstrap loss versus the dual objective, or the modified spectral layers versus a standard FNO. Excluding Amos et al. (2022) because its original setup is dataset-dependent does not resolve this: comparison at a common resolution using the same generated training distribution would directly test the proposed advantages.

The claims about accurate plans and Wasserstein geometry exceed the quantitative evidence. Appendix D.6 usefully reports marginal violations, but small transport-cost error does not establish proximity to the optimal coupling. Barycenters and flows are assessed mainly through selected visual examples, and the GeONet superiority claim relies on a single displayed pair. Aggregate barycenter objective gaps, interpolation errors, and quantitative coupling comparisons are needed to support these broader conclusions.

The state-of-the-art efficiency claim needs a stronger comparison. Runtime tables use a ground-truth transport-cost error threshold rather than a joint accuracy and feasibility criterion, and exclude Gaussian and learned competing initializations from matched timing comparisons. Speedups quoted from other papers do not provide a controlled substitute. UNOT is slower on MNIST, and the 35-hour training cost is not related to an expected amortization workload. The evidence supports promising speedups over the tested default implementation, but not the full efficiency claim.
